answer: Applying \(|A+B+C|\ge |A|-|B|-|C|\) yields \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\ge |a_n|-|b_n|-|c_n|\). Since \(|a_n|=4^{-n}|\cos(160n\,x_n)-\cos(160n\,c)|\ge 4^{-n}\), while \(|b_n|\le \frac{4}{13}4^{-n}\) and \(|c_n|\le \frac{2}{3}4^{-n}\), we obtain \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\ge \frac{1}{39}4^{-n}\). Dividing by \(|x_n-c|\le \frac{3\pi}{160n}\) gives the same unbounded lower bound as above.

question: If a sequence \((x_n)\) satisfies \(|x_n-c|\to 0\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), explain why \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\to 0\), and how this fact is used to argue that the difference quotient cannot converge to a finite limit, thereby proving that the function is nowhere differentiable.
answer: Since \(|x_n-c|\to 0\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), we have \(f(x_n)\to f(c)\), so \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|\to 0\). If the difference quotient converged to a finite limit, the sequence \(\left|\frac{f(x_n)-f(c)}{x_n-c}\right|\) would be bounded, contradicting the unbounded lower bound derived earlier. Hence the quotient cannot converge, proving the function is nowhere differentiable.

question: Using the inequality \(|\cos x-\cos y|\le |x|\;|x-y|\) and the fact that \(|\cos(160k\,x)|\le 1\), explain why the function \(f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) is uniformly continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).
answer: Because each term satisfies \(|\cos(160k\,x)-\cos(160k\,y)|\le 160k\,|x-y|\), the difference of the \(k\)-th term in the series is bounded by \(\frac{160k}{4^{k}}|x-y|\). Summing over \(k\) gives a Lipschitz constant \(L=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{160k}{4^{k}}=160\cdot\frac{4}{9}=\frac{640}{9}\). Thus \(f\) is Lipschitz (hence uniformly continuous) on \(\mathbb{R}\).

question: The lecture states that for every real \(x\) the series \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) converges absolutely. Explain why this guarantees that the function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by this series is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).
answer: Since \(|\cos(160k\,x)/4^{k}|\le 1/4^{k}\) and \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}1/4^{k}=4/3\) converges, the series converges absolutely for every real \(x\). Absolute convergence of a series of continuous functions implies uniform convergence on \(\mathbb{R}\), and a uniformly convergent series of continuous functions has a continuous sum. Therefore \(f\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\).

question: Using the definition of continuity as the equality \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\), explain why the implication \(\displaystyle f\text{ differentiable at }c\;\Rightarrow\;f\text{ continuous at }c\) holds. In particular, identify which part of the definition is directly employed in the proof and discuss whether the converse could be deduced from the definition alone.
answer: The proof uses the fact that if \(f\) is differentiable at \(c\), then the limit \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\) exists and equals \(f'(c)\). Multiplying this limit by \((x-c)\) and adding \(f(c)\) yields \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\), which is exactly the definition of continuity. Thus the definition’s requirement that the limit of \(f(x)\) equals \(f(c)\) is the part that is invoked. The converse cannot be inferred from the definition alone because continuity only guarantees the limit of \(f(x)\) exists and equals \(f(c)\); it says nothing about the existence of the limit of the difference quotient, which is needed for differentiability.

question: The lecture discusses that \(f\) is continuous and bounded. Using the definition of limit, explain why for any sequence \((x_n)\) converging to a point \(c\), the sequence \((f(x_n))\) converges to \(f(c)\).
answer: Continuity at \(c\) means that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|x-c|<\delta\) implies \(|f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\). Since \(x_n\to c\), for large \(n\) we have \(|x_n-c|<\delta\), hence \(|f(x_n)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\). Thus \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)=f(c)\).

question: Given the precise definition of continuity at a point \(c\) as \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\), analyze why the converse of "differentiability at \(c\) implies continuity at \(c\)" does not hold in general.
answer: The definition of continuity requires only that the function values approach the function value at \(c\). Differentiability, on the other hand, requires the existence of the limit of the difference quotient \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\). Continuity does not impose any condition on the behavior of this quotient, so a continuous function may have a sharp corner or cusp where the quotient limit does not exist. Hence the converse fails.

question: Considering the definition of a limit as the value a function approaches, discuss why the existence of \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\) (i.e., continuity) does not guarantee that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\) exists, thereby invalidating the converse of the differentiability‑implies‑continuity theorem.
answer: The limit \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to c}f(x)=f(c)\) guarantees that the function values settle at \(f(c)\) as \(x\) approaches \(c\). But differentiability demands that the scaled difference \(\frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}\) also stabilizes to a finite value. Continuity alone does not control the rate of change of \(f\) near \(c\); the quotient can oscillate or diverge even when the function itself is continuous. Thus the existence of the continuity limit does not imply the existence of the derivative limit, invalidating the converse.

question: The function \(f\) is shown to be bounded by \(\frac{4}{3}\). Explain how the fact that each term \(\frac{\cos(160k x)}{4^k}\) is bounded by \(4^{-k}\) and the series converges leads to this bound, referencing the definition of a bounded function.

question: In the lecture, the function \(g(x)=\cos(kx)\) maps an interval of length \(2\pi/k\) onto the real numbers between \(-1\) and \(1\). The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) converges absolutely for every real \(x\). Explain how the absolute convergence of this series ensures that the function \(f(x)=\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) takes real values for all \(x\), and how the fact that the range of \(g(x)\) is \([-1,1]\) helps establish that \(f\) is bounded by a real number.
answer: Because each term \(\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) is a real number and the series of absolute values \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{|\cos(160k\,x)|}{4^{k}}\) converges (since \(|\cos|\le 1\) and \(\sum 1/4^{k}=4/3\)), the sum \(f(x)\) converges to a real limit for every real \(x\). The mapping property of \(g(x)=\cos(kx)\) guarantees that every term lies in \([-1,1]\), so the partial sums are bounded by \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}1/4^{k}=4/3\). Thus \(f(x)\) is a real‑valued function bounded above by the real number \(4/3\).

question: Using the definition of a function as an association of a single output to each input, and the definition of absolute value as a function measuring size, explain why the absolute convergence of the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) guarantees that the function \(f(x)\) defined by this series is bounded by a real number, and how this boundedness is employed in the limsup argument to prove continuity of \(f\).
answer: The absolute convergence of \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\cos(160k\,x)}{4^{k}}\) means that \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{|\cos(160k\,x)|}{4^{k}}\) converges to a finite real number (at most \(4/3\)). Hence each partial sum of the original series is a real number, and the limit \(f(x)\) is a real number for every \(x\). The bound \(4/3\) provides a uniform real upper bound for \(|f(x)|\) over all \(x\). In the limsup argument for continuity, this bound allows us to control the tail of the series uniformly, ensuring that the difference \(f(x_n)-f(c)\) can be made arbitrarily small for \(x_n\to c\), thereby proving continuity.
